title: The Vishuddha chakra in the destiny matrix: a voice between head and heart

seo.title: Vishuddha in the destiny matrix: the meaning of its three arcana
seo.description: Vishuddha in the destiny matrix: find its three numbers by date of birth, read arcana 3 to 22 in each column and see why the throat sits between head and heart.

short: Vishuddha in the destiny matrix is the fifth chakra. On our energy map it comes straight after Anahata: from closeness to the word. Its theme is speech and influence. The three numbers of the row answer three questions: how you speak, what you enter a conversation for, and what happens inside you when the answer comes. Physics is the chart’s inner left point J (the day arcanum plus the centre), energy is the inner point of talent K (the month plus the centre), and emotions are their sum.

sections.h2: Finding your Vishuddha from your date of birth
paragraphs: You need five numbers from the matrix and three more additions. One rule holds for the whole calculation: if a sum is greater than 22, add up its digits (29 → 11, 40 → 4), and keep going until you get a number from 1 to 22.
Take 31 March 1993 as an example.

If you already know the centre of your matrix, it is simpler still: Vishuddha is “day plus centre” and “month plus centre”. In the calculator the whole table of seven chakras appears as soon as you enter a date — free and with no sign-up.

On the matrix diagram these two numbers sit on the left and top rays, in the third of five points counting from the edge towards the centre. Other guides put it as “one point on the horizontal line, the other on the vertical” — they mean the same cells, J and K.

sections.h2: Why Vishuddha is called the throat of the matrix
paragraphs: The throat is the narrow passage between head and heart: thought and feeling have to pass through it to become words. In the destiny matrix this is not a metaphor but the order of the calculation. The left and top rays of the chart each carry five points from the edge to the centre, and the chakras take them in turn: Sahasrara on the edge, then Ajna, Vishuddha and Anahata, with Manipura at the centre.

Vishuddha’s numbers are worked out before its neighbours’, straight from the edge of the chart and its centre. Only then do they give Ajna (edge plus Vishuddha) and Anahata (Vishuddha plus centre). The head and the heart of the matrix cannot be calculated without the throat.
The same calculation shows what your voice is made of.

**Physics: the calling card the centre speaks through.** J = A + E. In the matrix the day arcanum is the calling card: the first impression and your usual way of making contact. The centre is your main inner state, the comfort zone. Vishuddha’s physics joins the two: this is how you sound when there was no time to prepare a role and you speak as you are. It is easiest to hear in a heated argument, in answer to an unexpected question, in the first sentence after a pause. In the “Karmic task before 40” section of the reading, the same point J is read as your habitual way of matching the image you show with your inner footing.
**Energy: talent on its way out.** K = B + E, and it is the last point of the talent line. The line itself runs down the energy column of the three upper chakras:

head: Chakra
Energy
Place in the talent line
What it shows
rows: the form of work that suits it
**what the gift becomes once it has matured**

paragraphs: Talent comes down from above, from idea to form, and goes out to people through the throat. Vishuddha’s energy is ability in its finished state: no longer something to show off or prove, just something you calmly use. That is why the question “what do you speak up for?” almost coincides here with “what is your gift?”. The Hierophant in energy wants to pass on knowledge, the Star to give back hope, the World to translate some people into the language of others. When your work lets you speak for that, the words come easily. When it does not, being tired of talking often turns out to be tiredness with someone else’s goal.

**The centre sounds in both numbers.** E goes into J and into K alike. And the centre of the matrix is also Manipura, the chakra of will. In this system the voice grows from the same place as the will: what is inside is what comes out in words.

**Its mirror pair is Svadhisthana.** The matrix has four inner points. The left and top ones, J and K, go to Vishuddha; the right and bottom ones, L and M, go to Svadhisthana, the chakra of desire and pleasure. One wants, the other speaks: two halves of one inner square.

sections.h2: Vishuddha in tradition: sixteen vowels and the white moon of ether
paragraphs: The chakra’s name comes from the Sanskrit viśuddha, “especially pure”. The best-known old description is in Purnananda’s treatise Shat-chakra-nirupana (1577), which English readers know from John Woodroffe’s translation in The Serpent Power (1919). There Vishuddha looks like this:

ul: a lotus in the throat, “of a smoky purple hue”;
sixteen petals, each carrying one of the sixteen vowels of Sanskrit;
in the middle, a circular region of ether, akasha, “white like the full Moon”;
the chakra’s syllable is HAM, seated on an elephant “white as snow”;
of the one who has mastered this chakra, the text says that he becomes “eloquent and wise”.

paragraphs: The detail about the vowels is one to remember. A consonant gives a word its shape, but a vowel can be drawn out by the voice — the sound rests on it. The petals of the throat carry the voice of the alphabet. Ether was not chosen by chance either: in Indian philosophy its quality is sound. The blue that Vishuddha is painted in today came much later, in Western books of the 20th century, where the chakras were given the colours of the rainbow.

In Benebell Wen’s Holistic Tarot (2015), card 5 of the Seven Chakras Spread corresponds with the throat chakra and “denotes expression, community, and communication”. From this card she reads “how the Seeker expresses his or her views” and “the Seeker’s relationship to others and how the Seeker expresses or communicates that relationship”. The destiny matrix is not a spread: instead of one drawn card we have three calculated arcana, each with a question of its own. But the question of the fifth chakra is the same — what happens when what is inside gets said.

sections.h2: Vishuddha’s three columns: how you speak, why, and what you feel
paragraphs: The columns of the energy map have the same names in every row — physics, energy, emotions. But in each chakra they ask a question of their own. In Vishuddha it goes like this.

**Physics is delivery.** How a thought turns into words: directly or gently, briefly or with examples, through facts or through images. It is what the other person hears before they have even grasped the meaning. The test question: how do I talk when there is no time to choose my words?

**Energy is motive.** Why you start talking at all: to reach a decision, to keep someone close, to pass on knowledge, to name the truth, to make people laugh. The same calm tone can serve different ends, and sooner or later the other person senses which one. The question: what do I want from this conversation?

**Emotions are the response.** What the answer does to you: pleases, stings, calms, will not let go. Emotions are the sum of the first two numbers, and in life you can see it plainly: how you take an answer grows out of how you spoke and what for. Whoever wanted a decision waits for a “yes”. Whoever wanted to be understood waits for recognition. The question: what do I feel when the other person answers — or says nothing?
The arcana that come up most often in the emotions column are the Hierophant, the Lovers and the Chariot — each at about 9% of dates. The rarest is Death: about 1%.

The main rule of reading: three numbers make one scene, not three separate traits. The row 8 / 7 / 15 is not “honesty, drive and dependence”. It is a person who weighs every word, steers an argument to a clear agreement and then cannot let go of someone else’s “no” for a long time. How numbers add up to a scene like this is shown after the reference.

sections.h2: The arcana in Vishuddha: meanings from 3 to 22
paragraphs: Find your three numbers and read the lines you need: physics for the first number, energy for the second, emotions for the third. “Where it goes wrong” describes how the strength of the arcanum starts to get in the way of a conversation. It is a possible scenario, not a verdict.
The Magician (1) and the High Priestess (2) never appear in any column of Vishuddha. The reason is in the questions at the end of the article.

ul: **Physics.** Warm, vivid speech: an example instead of a rule, support before advice. People feel calmer after talking to you. In physics the Empress is rare — about 2% of dates.

**Energy.** The wish for something to grow out of the conversation: a person’s confidence, an idea, a shared project. The rarest energy in Vishuddha: across the years 1900–2099 it goes to one single date — 1 August 2000.
**Emotions.** Warmth when a word takes root: the advice came in useful, the person blossomed, came back with a result.
**Where it goes wrong.** Care starts deciding for the other person what it is time for them to know. An unpleasant truth is softened beyond recognition, and the other person gets a filtered picture.
**Physics.** Speaking point by point: terms, deadlines, who is responsible for what. After a conversation with you it is clear what to do next. Rare — about 2% of dates.
**Energy.** To bring order and share out responsibility: everyone gets their part of the job, your own people get protection. A rare energy, about 0.6% of dates.
**Emotions.** The calm of certainty: there is a frame, the roles are clear. What unsettles you is agreements starting to drift.
**Where it goes wrong.** Discussion turns into handing out orders. A rule has to be explained again, and irritation grows faster than understanding.
**Physics.** Explaining what everything rests on: why things are done this way, what has been tested, what the lesson is. You speak a shared language, and people trust you.

**Energy.** To pass on knowledge: to teach, to make someone else’s experience understandable, to keep the meaning of what is passing away. Among the meanings of this card Waite lists “the man to whom the Querent has recourse”.

**Emotions.** Satisfaction when you were understood and the advice came in useful; your footing is the agreement of your own circle. The most common arcanum in Vishuddha’s emotions, almost 10% of dates.
**Where it goes wrong.** Advice starts to sound compulsory. If it is not taken, it hurts as if you yourself had been rejected — and teaching quietly turns into lecturing.
**Physics.** Speaking as a partner: as equals, one to one, without masks. Your words are fair to both of you.
**Energy.** To come to an agreement and stay on the same side. You need the conversation for the bond, not for the win.
**Emotions.** The joy of a match: a mutual “yes”, making up after a falling-out.
**Where it goes wrong.** Any disagreement feels like a threat to the relationship. A convenient “yes” is said for the sake of peace, and the real “no” piles up until the first quarrel.
**Physics.** Speech that leads to a goal: short, direct, with a clear next step. You know how to steer a discussion to an outcome.
**Energy.** To get a question moving: to bring the conversation to a decision, to close what has dragged on.
**Emotions.** The thrill of moving forward and the triumph of a “yes”.

**Where it goes wrong.** The other person has not yet understood the task, and you are already at the next turn. A pause feels like defeat, the conversation becomes a race, and the agreement is wrung out rather than shared.
**Physics.** Precision: facts without exaggeration, terms without guile, a claim kept apart from a guess.
**Energy.** To speak honestly and to the point, so that everything falls into place for both sides.
**Emotions.** Relief when the conversation ends in an honest result.

**Where it goes wrong.** Precision turns into a trial: who is right, who is to blame, where the other person put it inaccurately. The record is flawless, and the person opposite feels like the accused.
**Physics.** Precision in few words. You speak when the thought is thought through, and you can listen without interrupting.

**Energy.** First to work it out for yourself, then to share what you found. Waite describes the Hermit’s lantern as a beacon that says “where I am, you also may be”. In Vishuddha this is the wish to light the way for someone else with what you have been through yourself.
**Emotions.** A deep, unhurried response: an answer needs to ripen in private.

**Where it goes wrong.** The pause drags on, the other person does not know what you think and decides for you. What you left unsaid seems obvious to you — and it surprises you that nobody understood it.
**Physics.** A sense of the moment: your words adjust to a new turn, and you know when to speak up.
**Energy.** An interest in live exchange — in the unexpected question and in where the talk will turn.
**Emotions.** A lift from the twists of a conversation — and a swing: hope, doubt, hope again.
**Where it goes wrong.** Your position shifts with the mood of the conversation. A promise made on one turn is forgotten on the next, and people struggle to tell which of your words they can rely on.

**Physics.** Firmness without pressure: calmly holding your ground and saying “no” without raising your voice. On Waite’s card a woman gently closes a lion’s mouth — for the throat chakra the image is almost literal. Waite even noted that in the earlier form of the card “she is obviously opening it”, and judged the closing gesture “better symbolically”. The most common arcanum in Vishuddha’s physics — almost 7% of dates.
**Energy.** To withstand someone else’s pressure and not drop your thought: soft steadiness instead of a counter-blow.
**Emotions.** A strong response you manage to hold: the wave rises — and becomes a boundary, not an attack.
**Where it goes wrong.** Restraint builds up until it flares, or sets into stubbornness: “I am calm, but I will not move an inch.”
**Physics.** Hearing someone out and checking back: saying how you understood them, looking at the question from the other side.
**Energy.** To understand someone else’s truth, putting your ready answer aside.
**Emotions.** Sympathy for the other person’s side, and a pause after which the answer looks different.
**Where it goes wrong.** In conversation there is only ever room for someone else’s story. Your own answer stays outside the door, and a quiet resentment builds up that nobody knows about.
**Physics.** Ending clearly: putting a full stop, speaking plainly about a change, closing an argument that has run its course.
**Energy.** To let go of what has outlived itself: a role, a formula, familiar phrases that no longer work.
**Emotions.** Living through an ending — with sadness and with the relief of final clarity. The rarest arcanum in Vishuddha’s emotions, about 1% of dates.
**Where it goes wrong.** The full stop comes abruptly and without explanation. Or it never comes at all, and a conversation that ended long ago drags on out of fear of saying “that’s it”.
**Physics.** A soft, even tone and carefully chosen words: unhurried, but clear.

**Energy.** To join different positions and find a third way. Waite writes that the rule of this card “tempers, combines and harmonises” the psychic and material natures. In Vishuddha this is the wish to bring the incompatible together in one conversation. One of the most common energies, about 7.5% of dates.
**Emotions.** Taking any answer evenly and quickly getting your balance back.
**Where it goes wrong.** For the sake of peace, the very difference the decision depends on gets smoothed over. Everything is agreed, everyone is happy — and the main thing is never named.
**Physics.** Speaking plainly about what is wanted: naming the gain, the interest, the temptation — what people usually keep quiet about. Your speech is magnetic and persuasive.
**Energy.** A strong wish to influence, to carry people along, to get your way. The most common arcanum in Vishuddha’s energy, about 7.6% of dates.
**Emotions.** Attachment to the answer: pleasure when your words worked, and a tight grip when you were refused.

**Where it goes wrong.** Self-interest hides behind “I’m only advising”, influence turns into hidden pressure, and a refusal into defeat. An interest named out loud stops tugging at the conversation in secret.
**Physics.** Saying out loud what everyone walks around: a broken promise, the gap between words and deeds, pretence.

**Energy.** To stop playing at order and bring down a facade held up by things left unsaid. Among the old titles of this card Waite gives “the Tower of Babel”, and he calls it “assuredly a card of confusion”. Babel is the story of how people stopped understanding each other. The Tower in Vishuddha wants people to understand each other for real, even at the cost of a collapse.
**Emotions.** A sharp reaction to falseness: a flare-up when words never became deeds.
**Where it goes wrong.** The truth sounds like a verdict on the person rather than a statement of fact. The blow brings relief, but afterwards there is nobody left to talk to.
**Physics.** Vivid speech, a story, support for someone else’s plan: you speak so that a person sees what is possible.
**Energy.** To pass on hope — to bring back the belief that it will work out.
**Emotions.** Inspiration from a response, joy in someone else’s hope.
**Where it goes wrong.** A beautiful image runs ahead of what you are ready to do. And if the other person does not share your picture of the future, the disappointment is stronger than any argument.
**Physics.** Carefully finding words for something hazy: asking back, separating what was heard from what only seemed to be said.
**Energy.** To hear what lies under the words: tone, pauses, what is left unsaid.
**Emotions.** Sensitivity to half-tones — and anxiety when the answer is unclear or the other person goes quiet.
**Where it goes wrong.** A guess about a hidden meaning is taken for fact. An inner dialogue for two replaces one simple question: “Is that what you meant?”
**Physics.** Openly, simply and in front of everyone: saying what you want, acknowledging someone else’s success, voicing a thought with no hidden agenda.
**Energy.** To share what delights you and lights you up — and to be heard.
**Emotions.** Joy when you are understood: that very “got it!” in the other person’s eyes.
**Where it goes wrong.** Performing crowds out conversation, and there is no room left for anyone else’s answer. A calm reaction from listeners hurts like coldness.
**Physics.** Saying your piece about what matters: naming a decision that is overdue, summing up, calling for reconciliation.

**Energy.** To answer an inner call and speak about what has lasting meaning. On this card everything begins with a sound: the angel blows the trumpet, and the dead rise. Waite asks: “What is that within us which does sound a trumpet and all that is lower in our nature rises in response—almost in a moment, almost in the twinkling of an eye?”
**Emotions.** Relief when the important thing is finally named; someone else’s answer comes as an awakening.

**Where it goes wrong.** Every conversation becomes a trial of the past. Or the other way round: your own voice drowns in familiar family judgements, and having an opinion of your own feels like betrayal.
**Physics.** Translating from one language to another: explaining some people to others, finding words for every circle — different professions, generations, views.
**Energy.** To gather everyone into a shared meaning, so that nobody is left out.
**Emotions.** Satisfaction when the whole picture comes together and different people understand each other.
**Where it goes wrong.** Talk about the whole hides the specifics: the big picture is drawn, but who does what by Friday is never said.
**Physics.** A simple question out loud, a joke, trying out a phrasing on the fly — speech without armour.
**Energy.** Conversation without a script: curiosity about the other person, the courage not to know the answer in advance.
**Emotions.** Lightness before any answer, even a refusal.
**Where it goes wrong.** A joke stands in for an answer. Being asked to make clear where the joke ends and the promise begins feels like an attack on your freedom.

sections.h2: Why three meanings from a reference are not yet a reading
paragraphs: A reference says what each arcanum does on its own. In a living person the arcana do not just stand side by side — they change one another. Here is the Devil, for many the most alarming card, in six different Vishuddhas. On the right are the titles and key thoughts of the interpretations in the full reading.

head: Numbers
Where the Devil is
Interpretation in the reading
Key thought
rows: “Words that bind people to a promise”
After your message, a vague “later” becomes a commitment that gets kept.
Your “why not?” can thaw someone who has long lived on nothing but “I have to”.
You can stay close to strong tension without letting it control your words.
“Helping a loved one believe in themselves again”
In your words, a person sees themselves as strong again.
“Steering a conversation to a clear decision”
You can turn an argument into an agreement where everyone knows what they have signed up to.
“Seeing the circle and stepping out of it”
A repetition named out loud loses some of its power.

paragraphs: One arcanum, six different people. Next to Justice and the Chariot, the Devil becomes someone else’s answer that holds on longer than the conversation itself. Next to Temperance and Strength, it is a pull towards a sharp exchange you can hardly tear yourself away from. Next to the Star, a stubborn wish to help someone close believe in themselves. Paired with itself, a gift for talking a person into joy. From the dictionary’s “temptation and dependence” you cannot get to a single one of these pictures.

That is why the full reading has no dictionary. A separate text has been written for each of the 379 combinations that occur among people born from 1900 to 2099. It has three parts: what your Vishuddha is about, how the combination looks in life, and where it starts to get in the way.

paragraphs.h3: What an interpretation looks like: the 8 / 7 / 15 example

paragraphs: This is how the Vishuddha section looks in the reading for 31.03.1993.
**Steering a conversation to a clear decision**

head: Physics
Energy
Emotions
rows: 7 · The Chariot — driving talk towards a result
15 · The Devil — a reply that won’t let go

paragraphs: Your speech carries the scales and sword of Justice: your words are weighed, and what you say cuts through confusion. You call things by their names, hear both sides out and even say no with your reasons attached. It is the Chariot that draws you into a conversation: talking is a journey with a destination, and you want to steer it past every objection to an outcome. And the other person’s reply goes deep — that is the Devil of your Vishuddha: someone else’s “yes” or “no” can hold you longer than the conversation itself lasted.

The group chat has spent three days arguing over who pays what for a trip together. The messages multiply, and so do the grievances. You write one message: who takes on what, why that’s fair and the date to settle it all by. **You can turn an argument into an agreement where everyone knows what they have signed up to.** The thread ends in a to-do list rather than a row, and the others’ agreement grips you like a small victory you keep wanting to relive.

But what if a well-weighed argument is turned down? The reasoning is fair, the road to the goal is clear — and the answer is still “no”. The Chariot doesn’t like standing still, and the conversation easily turns into a contest where the point is no longer to agree but to be proven right. Someone else’s refusal holds you like a chain: in the evening you replay the conversation, find new arguments, read motives into their words that may never have been there. A solution may well be found, but trust gets left somewhere halfway down the road.

Compare this with what a reference would give you: “honesty, drive, attachment”. All true, but the scene — a person who ends a three-day argument with one message and in the evening replays someone else’s “no” — is nowhere in those words.

sections.h2: A “blocked Vishuddha”: what the numbers really show
paragraphs: Popular articles on chakras carry lists of “signs of a blocked Vishuddha”, from a fear of speaking in public to the proverbial lump in the throat. The numbers of the matrix show nothing of the kind. An arcanum is a symbol, not a score. Every cell of the table is filled, and there is no number that would mean “the chakra is blocked” or “in the minus”. The Devil in emotions is no worse than the Sun, and Death in physics is no more dangerous than the Empress.
What the numbers do show is something else: where a conversation can break down. When Vishuddha falters, the trouble almost always sits in one of the three columns.

head: Where it broke
What it looks like
Which number to read
rows: it came out harsher, softer or longer than you meant; the right thought sounded wrong
the conversation began for the sake of a decision and went on for the sake of being right, of quiet or of approval
after someone else’s “no” there is nothing left to say; the other person’s silence is louder than their words

paragraphs: How to find where yours falters. Recall a recent conversation that left you feeling “they didn’t hear me”. Reconstruct what was actually said — the words themselves, not their meaning. Work out where it broke: in the words, in the goal or in how you took the answer. Then read “Where it goes wrong” for the arcanum in that column. Most often what you find there is not someone else’s fault but your own strength, which overdid it this time.

ul: **Reading the number as a grade.** 22 is not “stronger” than 3, and 15 is not “more dangerous” than 6. The number is the name of a symbol, not an amount of energy.

**Taking the general meaning of the arcanum instead of its column.** The Devil in Vishuddha’s emotions is not “dependence in general” but attachment to the other person’s answer. The Chariot in physics is not “travel” but speech that leads to a goal.
**Gluing three meanings into a list.** “Honest, driven, dependent” is three dictionary entries, not a person. The reading begins when a single scene comes into view.

**Carrying names over from another system.** The destiny matrix uses the old Marseille numbering: 8 is Justice, 11 is Strength. In Waite’s deck and in many tarot books these two cards trade places — Waite himself wrote that he made the swap “for reasons which satisfy myself”. The meaning rests on the name of the card: in someone else’s reference, look up not the number but Justice or Strength.
**Looking for a forecast in Vishuddha.** The row describes your way of speaking, your motive and your response. It says nothing about events — who will say what, how an argument will end.

paragraphs: The matrix calculation is free and needs no sign-up. As soon as you enter a date you see the whole “Chakras and your arcana” table: seven rows, three arcana in each. Vishuddha is the fifth row of our table.

The interpretation opens in the full reading. There each chakra has a section of its own, as in the 8 / 7 / 15 example: the name of the combination, captions for the three arcana and a connected text — what this chakra is about for you, how the combination looks in life and where it starts to get in the way. All 379 variants of Vishuddha are written this way, and so are all the combinations of the other six chakras. The full reading is paid for once, with no subscription, and includes all 20 sections — from money and relationships to the reading by decades.

sections.h2: What this guide is based on

ul: **Calculation** — the classic destiny matrix scheme with points A–T: D = A + B + C, E = A + B + C + D, Vishuddha’s physics J = A + E, energy K = B + E, emotions their sum; every number over 22 is reduced by adding its digits. The list of combinations and the most common and rarest variants were counted by going through every day from 1900 to 2099; the shares of arcana in the columns, through the dates from 1900 to 2025.

**Card imagery** — A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910, reissued 1922): Strength, the Hermit, Temperance, Judgement, the old titles of the Tower, the lists of meanings for the Magician, the High Priestess and the Hierophant. Quotations are given in Waite’s own words.
**The fifth position of the chakra spread** — Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015), chapter 14, “The Seven Chakras Spread”.
**Tradition** — Purnananda, Shat-chakra-nirupana (1577), verses 28–31, in the translation by Arthur Avalon (John Woodroffe), The Serpent Power (1919).

**Readings of the triples** — Arcana Sense’s own synthesis. Neither Waite nor Wen wrote about the destiny matrix, and neither describes physics / energy / emotions triples. Reading the row as one scene, the talent line in the energy of the upper chakras as “the gift coming down to the throat”, and every “Where it goes wrong” are our interpretation.

The destiny matrix is an esoteric model for self-observation with no scientific evidence behind it. The strengths and difficulties described here can be compared with your own experience; they do not describe the body and do not determine whether chakras are “open”.

intro: This row has two features that almost nobody writes about. In the calculation Vishuddha literally stands between head and heart: both Ajna and Anahata are built from its numbers. And its energy is the very point K where the talent line ends. In the matrix, voice and gift meet in one point.

intro: Your Vishuddha is the fifth row of the table. Enter your date of birth to see your three arcana.

faq.q: How do you read Vishuddha in the destiny matrix?
faq.a: Work out the three numbers — physics is the day plus the centre, energy is the month plus the centre, emotions are their sum — or take them from the calculator. Read each one in its own column of the reference: the first is how you speak, the second what for, the third what you feel in response. Then put them together into one scene: what kind of conversation is typical for you and where it usually breaks down. The ready-made interpretation of your whole combination is in the full reading.

faq.q: What does it mean if physics and energy have the same number?
faq.a: This happens for about one date in sixteen. Most often it is when the day arcanum equals the number of the month: 5 May, 12 December, 23 May (23 → 5), 30 March (30 → 3). A repeat does not double the quality. One arcanum answers two different questions: how you speak and what for. Strength in both columns is a calm voice that never shouts and also the wish not to drop your thought under pressure.

faq.q: Why are the Magician and the High Priestess never found in Vishuddha?
faq.a: Because of the arithmetic. All three Vishuddha numbers include the centre of the chart, and the centre is itself a sum of four numbers and is never below 3. So neither physics, nor energy, nor emotions can drop below the Empress. There is an irony in this: among the Magician’s meanings Waite lists “skill, diplomacy”, and among the High Priestess’s, “silence”. The master of the word and the keeper of silence never turn up in the chakra of speech. It is a play of numbers, not a law, but it sticks in the mind.

faq.q: Which Vishuddha is the most common, and which is the rarest?
faq.a: People born from 1900 to 2099 get 379 different combinations. By variety this is the second row of the table after Anahata; Manipura, for comparison, has only 16 combinations. The most common is 11 / 14 / 7, yet even it goes to just one date in 182. The rarest is 5 / 3 / 8: in two hundred years exactly one day gets it, 1 August 2000.

faq.q: Is Vishuddha connected with the throat and the voice?
faq.a: Only as an image. The throat in the name “throat chakra” is its traditional place, not information about the body. The numbers of the matrix say nothing about timbre, volume or how you sing. They describe your manner of conversation, its motive and your response — things you can recognise in your own words.

faq.q: Is Vishuddha different for men and women?
faq.a: No. Gender does not affect the calculation: with the same date of birth the numbers are the same, and so is the interpretation. If an article gives a “female Vishuddha” tasks of its own, those are the author’s views, not the formula of the matrix.

faq.q: Can you “open” or “level up” your Vishuddha?
faq.a: The numbers do not change — they are calculated from the date of birth. What changes is how you handle your arcana. Each has a side where it helps and a side where it gets in the way: “Where it goes wrong” in the reference is about the second. In this sense, working with Vishuddha is very practical: notice your typical slip and next time do one step differently — hear the person out, name your interest out loud, don’t explain for the third time.
